title: Reeds, tone and embouchure
summary: Plastic reeds, Albert and Boehm systems, tone coming from the lip, and advice on embouchure.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: I see you have a plastic reed. Do you think they work all right?

Yes, sir. You know, those are the old ten-cent reeds. We used to have them go two for a quarter, three for a quarter. Sometimes they get thick up in your shirt, and then you wouldn't have no reed to play, see? Yeah. And you have to get the nickel and put two nickels together to get it even, see? And get a cigarette, imagine light it up, it's quite even.
I've seen people do that. Do you like the Albert system better? Did you ever try the Bain system? I tried.
I couldn't do no business with him. I couldn't do no business.
Do you think this has a better tone than the other one?
No, the tone is that, it's not the instrument. The tone is in the lip.
Do you have any advice for a young kid that would be starting clarinet? Would you advise him to take up the Albert system, or?

Well, I would advise them how to use the reed, the pressure on the reed. What would they do to get a good tone? Well, you see, they get a good tone, I find it. It's simple. Sure. Now, the fellow that uses his teeth, he don't have good pressure like the one that don't.
You know what I mean? Cover your lip over it. Yeah, you see your teeth, kills that tonation, the teeth. Yeah. But by not having none, well, your tones come in.
In other words, you have better lip control when you use the lip.

Yeah. Well, you know, you need some repair. Some players, I know, put their upper teeth down there, and others, I think Barney Bigard uses what they call the French embouchure, putting both lips. Yeah, I think so, yeah. Oh, you advise that, putting both lips together?
Yeah, because you can, you can, if you have the slur, you can make that, what they call the lip slur. Lip slur. If you use the teeth.

Now, Bessier, he used that because he used to make a whole lot of things, he'd make you make an immediate chicken or something, you see. Well, he, and some other things he used to make. Comes from the lip. From the lips. Mm-hmm.

That's using his lips. Very controlling the lip. Well, somebody told me once, I believe Wilbur Swetman used to have an act, he'd play two clarinets at once, and then Sidney, he'd take his clarinet and he'd take one piece off at a time, you know, the bell. I used to do that, too. Yeah, and finally end up with the mouthpiece. Yeah, I used to do that, too. How long did you stay in Chicago with that band?
